Key ideas

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

Definitions

Free-falling: when a body is falling and the only force acting on the body is gravity
Parabolic path: an approximately U-shaped plane curve that is mirror-symmetrical. This is the path taken by a projectile that is only under the influence of gravity and air resistance is considered negligible.
Net force: the sum of all of the forces acting on an object

Formulas

Equations of constant acceleration

7C

New knowledgeDeriving the formulas for constant acceleration

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

When analysing straight-line motion, graphs are extremely useful.

From graphs, you can derive the formulas for constant straight-line acceleration shown below: These formulas can then be applied to problems involving constant acceleration to quickly find a solution.

An object moving with constant acceleration is represented by a diagonal line on a velocity–time graph that has a constant, non-zero, gradient.

For example, a cyclist accelerates at a constant rate of 2 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2 for 5 seconds.

Figure 7C–2 Velocity–time graph for a cyclist accelerating at 2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ for 5 seconds
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 433
7C

New knowledgeDeriving the formulas for constant acceleration

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

The velocity–time graph of the cyclist’s motion is shown in Figure 7C–2.

Let’s say you wanted to find the average velocity of the cyclist.

The distance travelled is the area under the graph, so d=12(5)(10)=25d = \frac{1}{2}(5)(10) = 25d=21​(5)(10)=25 m.

Now, to find the average velocity, the distance is divided by the time, so v=255=5v = \frac{25}{5} = 5v=525​=5 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 434
7C

New knowledgeDeriving the formulas for constant acceleration

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

Figure 7C–3 shows that even though the cyclist has an ever-changing velocity over time, they will cover the same distance in 5 seconds as a cyclist moving at a constant velocity of 5 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1.

Note that this average velocity is only applicable when the cyclist travels for 5 s.

The average velocity would be less if the cyclist were to travel for less than 5 s and greater if travelling more than 5 s with the same acceleration.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 435
7C

New knowledgeDeriving the formulas for constant acceleration (derivation)

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

As you learned earlier in this chapter, the gradient of a velocity–time graph is the acceleration: gradient=a=riserun=ΔvΔt=v−uΔt\text{gradient} = a = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v - u}{\Delta t}gradient=a=runrise​=ΔtΔv​=Δtv−u​ This can be rearranged to give: v=u+atv = u + atv=u+at This is one equation.

Now consider the motion of another cyclist that is initially riding at 6 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 and accelerates at a constant rate of 1 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2 for 5 s, as shown in Figure 7C–4.

As you learned earlier in this chapter, the area under a velocity–time graph is the displacement.

To find the displacement of the cyclist after their 5 s journey, the graph would have to be divided into a rectangle and a triangle.

Figure 7C–4 Displacement of a cyclist initially riding at 6 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and accelerating at 1 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ for 5 seconds
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 446
7C

New knowledgeDeriving the formulas for constant acceleration (derivation)

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

From Figure 7C–4, the displacement is given by: s=12t(v−u)+uts = \frac{1}{2}t(v - u) + uts=21​t(v−u)+ut All the other equations for uniform acceleration can be derived from this formula.

The equation can be expanded and simplified to: s=12tv−12tu+uts = \frac{1}{2}tv - \frac{1}{2}tu + uts=21​tv−21​tu+ut s=12(u+v)ts = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)ts=21​(u+v)t This is a second equation.

You have learned that the acceleration is given by: a=v−uta = \frac{v - u}{t}a=tv−u​ You can rearrange this to: at=v−uat = v - uat=v−u This means that atatat can be substituted for v−uv - uv−u giving: s=12t(v−u)+uts = \frac{1}{2}t(v - u) + uts=21​t(v−u)+ut s=12t(at)+uts = \frac{1}{2}t(at) + uts=21​t(at)+ut s=ut+12at2s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2s=ut+21​at2 This is a third equation.

The acceleration formula can then be rearranged to: t=v−uat = \frac{v - u}{a}t=av−u​ Then substituted into the equation as follows: s=12(u+v)ts = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)ts=21​(u+v)t s=u+v2(v−ua)s = \frac{u + v}{2}\left(\frac{v - u}{a}\right)s=2u+v​(av−u​) s=v2−u22as = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}s=2av2−u2​ v2=u2+2asv^2 = u^2 + 2asv2=u2+2as This is a fourth equation.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 447
7C

New knowledgeDeriving the formulas for constant acceleration (derivation)

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

The acceleration formula can be rearranged to: u=v−atu = v - atu=v−at It can then be substituted into the following equation: s=12(u+v)ts = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)ts=21​(u+v)t s=12(v−at+v)ts = \frac{1}{2}(v - at + v)ts=21​(v−at+v)t s=vt−12at2s = vt - \frac{1}{2}at^2s=vt−21​at2 This is a fifth equation.

All of the equations of constant acceleration are shown in Formula 7C–1.

Note: It is not a requirement to know how to derive these formulas.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 448
7C

New knowledgeHorizontal motion

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

Newton’s first law, which will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 8, states that a body in motion or at rest will remain in its state of motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.

This means that when a body moves horizontally through space, its velocity will not change unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.

Often objects will have a constant unbalanced force applied to them, like a car that is accelerating uniformly or a sprinter who is sprinting out of the blocks.

In these situations of uniform motion, the equations of motion can be applied.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 469
7C

New knowledgeHorizontal motion

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

When solving horizontal motion questions about objects with constant straight-line acceleration: • draw a diagram of the situation and put all the information that you have on the diagram in SI units • choose an appropriate equation based on the data that you have and the data that you need.

Remember that when vectors act in opposite directions, set one direction as positive; the opposite direction will then have a negative sign (except for t) • round your final answer to three significant figures.

Include units in your answer and, if your answer is a vector, a direction as well.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 4610
7C

New knowledgeVertical motion

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

When a body is launched vertically, and if air resistance is ignored, there is generally only one force acting on the body – the downwards force of gravity.

Close to the surface of Earth, the force due to gravity will cause all free-falling objects to accelerate at 9.8 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2 down, to the surface of Earth.

For example, imagine if a 1 kg mass and a 2 kg mass that are initially at rest are dropped and allowed to free-fall.

If air resistance is ignored, they will both reach a velocity of 9.8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 down after 1 second, and then reach a velocity of 19.6 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 down after 2 seconds.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 4711
7C

New knowledgeVertical motion

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

If the 1 kg and 2 kg masses are thrown up with a velocity of 19.6 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1, the two masses will accelerate downwards towards the surface of Earth.

After 1 second, the velocity of both masses would be reduced to 9.8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 up, and after 2 seconds the velocity of both masses would be reduced to zero.

Although there is no direct record of it, it is said that in the 1500s, Italian scientist Galileo Galilei dropped two objects off the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

Even though one of the objects was much lighter than the other, they both fell at the same rate, indicating that the acceleration on both masses is the same.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 4712
7C

New knowledgeVertical motion

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

In 1971, during the Apollo 15 Moon landing, astronaut David Scott dropped a feather and a hammer at the same time.

Since there was minimal air resistance on the Moon, both the feather and the hammer hit the ground at the same time.

These examples demonstrate that the acceleration close to the surface of Earth is unaffected by an object’s mass or velocity.

Both masses had the same change in velocity and even the masses that were travelling upwards had a change in their velocity equal to 9.8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 downwards every second.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 4713
7C

New knowledgeVertical motion

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

The steps to solving a vertical motion problem are the same as the steps to solving a horizontal motion problem.

However, in vertical motion problems there are a number of key things to remember that will assist in solving them (ignoring air resistance).

The constant acceleration acting on all free-falling bodies is 9.8 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2 down.

Gravity is usually given a negative sign in an equation of motion and velocities directed upwards are given a positive sign.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 4714
7C

New knowledgeVertical motion

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration

An object that is thrown upwards will slow down until it comes to a stop; gravity will then begin to bring the object back down to Earth.

The stationary point of an object that is projected up in the air is its maximum height and half of the total flight time if the object lands at the same level that it was launched.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 4715

We doUsing equations of constant acceleration

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration
A ball travels forward with a velocity 4.65 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1. As it rolls over the ground, it slows to a stop in 1.75 s. A force acts on the ball, causing a constant deceleration (negative acceleration). Calculate the distance the ball travels before coming to a stop.
Key idea · Equations of constant accelerationv=u+at,v2=u2+2as,s=12(u+v)t,s=ut+12at2,s=vt−12at2v = u + at,\quad v^2 = u^2 + 2as,\quad s = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)t,\quad s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2,\quad s = vt - \frac{1}{2}at^2v=u+at,v2=u2+2as,s=21​(u+v)t,s=ut+21​at2,s=vt−21​at2

Working

First draw a diagram of the situation with all of the appropriate data.
[diagram: t=1.75t = 1.75t=1.75 s, a=?a = ?a=?, u=4.65u = 4.65u=4.65 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1, s=?s = ?s=?]
Select the appropriate formula and solve the problem.
s=12(u+v)t=12(4.65+0)(1.75)=4.07s = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)t = \frac{1}{2}(4.65 + 0)(1.75) = 4.07s=21​(u+v)t=21​(4.65+0)(1.75)=4.07 m
4.07 m
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 46, Worked example 7C-122
7C

We doVertical motion from a drop

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration
A cliff diver of mass 76 kg jumps off a cliff that is 15.1 m tall. If the cliff diver has no velocity when he leaves the cliff, calculate the velocity of the diver the moment before he hits the water. Ignore the effects of air resistance.
Key idea · Equations of constant accelerationv=u+at,v2=u2+2as,s=12(u+v)t,s=ut+12at2,s=vt−12at2v = u + at,\quad v^2 = u^2 + 2as,\quad s = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)t,\quad s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2,\quad s = vt - \frac{1}{2}at^2v=u+at,v2=u2+2as,s=21​(u+v)t,s=ut+21​at2,s=vt−21​at2

Working

The first step is to determine which direction is positive. In this example, it is easier to take down as positive. The second step is to identify all of the information in the question:
m=76m = 76m=76 kg
s=15.1s = 15.1s=15.1 m
u=0u = 0u=0 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
a=9.8a = 9.8a=9.8 m s−2\text{m s}^{-2}m s−2
v=?v = ?v=?
The mass of the diver is included but is irrelevant to this question as the acceleration of gravity is the same on all objects. Once you have all the relevant information, find an appropriate formula and solve the equation.
v2=u2+2asv^2 = u^2 + 2asv2=u2+2as
v=u2+2asv = \sqrt{u^2 + 2as}v=u2+2as​
=(0)2+2(9.8)(15.1)= \sqrt{(0)^2 + 2(9.8)(15.1)}=(0)2+2(9.8)(15.1)​
=17.2= 17.2=17.2 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1
Note that since gravity was acting down and the displacement was in the down direction, both numbers have been given a positive sign.
17.2 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 (down)
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 49, Worked example 7C-223
7C

We doVertical motion from a throw

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration
A student throws a ball of mass 200 g into the air vertically upwards, with an initial velocity of 20 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1. When the ball leaves the student’s hand, it is already 1.22 m above the ground.
a Calculate the maximum height above the ground reached by the ball.
b Calculate the total flight time of the ball, assuming that the student catches the ball at a height of 1.22 m above the ground.
Key idea · Equations of constant accelerationv=u+at,v2=u2+2as,s=12(u+v)t,s=ut+12at2,s=vt−12at2v = u + at,\quad v^2 = u^2 + 2as,\quad s = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)t,\quad s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2,\quad s = vt - \frac{1}{2}at^2v=u+at,v2=u2+2as,s=21​(u+v)t,s=ut+21​at2,s=vt−21​at2

Working

a The first step is to draw a diagram with all of the information given.
There is another piece of important information to remember; when the maximum vertical height is reached, the velocity of the ball will be zero. This means if you consider the movement of the ball from when it is released to its maximum height, the final velocity of the ball will be zero.
With this piece of information, you can now apply an appropriate formula:
v2=u2+2asv^2 = u^2 + 2asv2=u2+2as
s=v2−u22as = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}s=2av2−u2​
=(0)2−(20)2(2)(−9.8)=20.4= \frac{(0)^2 - (20)^2}{(2)(-9.8)} = 20.4=(2)(−9.8)(0)2−(20)2​=20.4 m
This is the distance that the ball travelled before it reached its turning point; to get the maximum height the initial height of the ball must be added.
maximum height = 20.4 + 1.22 = 21.6 m
b This problem can be solved with the knowledge that the time to reach the maximum height is half of the total flight time, as the ball lands at the same height that it was launched. Therefore, you must choose an appropriate formula with time:
v=u+atv = u + atv=u+at
t=v−uat = \frac{v - u}{a}t=av−u​
=(0)−(20)(−9.8)=2.04= \frac{(0) - (20)}{(-9.8)} = 2.04=(−9.8)(0)−(20)​=2.04 s
total time =2.04×2=4.08= 2.04 \times 2 = 4.08=2.04×2=4.08 s
There is often more than one way of reaching a solution. When a projectile is in free-fall, there is symmetry in the projectiles upwards and downwards movement. When the ball is travelling upwards, its upwards velocity is reducing by 9.8 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 every second; in this case the ball will travel 20.4 m up before the ball no longer has any upwards velocity. After this momentary stationary point, the ball will then fall a distance of 20.4 m, which means that just before the ball is caught, it will be travelling down at 20 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1. This can then be used as the final velocity as follows.
t=v−uat = \frac{v - u}{a}t=av−u​
=(−20)−(20)(−9.8)=4.08= \frac{(-20) - (20)}{(-9.8)} = 4.08=(−9.8)(−20)−(20)​=4.08 s
a 21.6 m; b 4.08 s
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 7, p. 50, Worked example 7C-324

You trySection 7C questions Q8a

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration
On a construction site of a new skyscraper, Sophia takes an open elevator up to the top floor. The elevator moves at a constant speed of 5 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1. As Sophia passes the third floor, she drops a wrench outside the elevator and onto the third floor. Sami is standing on the third floor and sees Sophia drop the wrench. Sophia states that in her point of view the wrench is falling down as soon as she drops it so Sami must also see the wrench falling down as soon as Sophia drops it.
a Comment on the accuracy of Sophia’s statement.

Working

Sophia’s statement is not correct. Relative to Sami, the wrench has an initial speed of 5 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 up when Sophia drops it. This means that Sami will initially see the wrench continue to move up.
7C Section questions.docx, 7C-SQ8a. Working from the worksheet answers.43
7C

You trySection 7C questions Q8b

Analysing straight-line motion with uniform acceleration
b At the exact moment that Sophia drops the wrench, Sami throws a bolt in the air with a speed of 5 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1. Which would land on the floor of the third floor first? Explain your answer.

Working

Both will hit the ground at the exact same time. This is because both of them have the same initial upwards velocity of 5 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1 and gravity is accelerating them both down at the same rate.

Working

The mass of the stone has no effect on its motion if air resistance is ignored. This is because the acceleration due to gravity is the same on all objects irrespective of their mass.
